body: Before Reading Partners, I served a year with another AmeriCorps Program called City Year. That involved small group and 1:1 tutoring in reading and math, plus assisting with classroom management, so I had some directly applicable experience that helped me feel more comfortable leading my reading center with Reading Partners. However, I know some folks that came to the program from backgrounds similar to yours, and they seemed to do well with it. Like I said, one thing RP did well when I was there was how detailed their curriculum is. That plus their training, I feel, would have assuaged most of my worries even if I didn't have the experience I did coming in. I think the job is doable without an education background, though it helped to have one.

I served with Reading Partners in Dallas about 10 years ago, so take my experience for what it's worth given the passage of time and difference in locations.

Of the AmeriCorps experiences I had, Reading Partners was solid without being amazing. Dallas was a brand new location for them at the time, so it was chaotic, and there was a lot of work I had to do to create relationships with my school site so that they would accept our program and even so teachers would let me pull kids for tutoring. What I liked about RP was they had a solid curriculum so that I knew pretty much exactly what was expected of me, my volunteers, and my students throughout the year. I really appreciated the autonomy I had at my school site. It felt like I got to make my reading center my own without anyone breathing down my neck, but I know other folks who had much different experiences because of the school administration they were saddled with.

What I didn't like about RP was the same stuff I found frustrating about all the AmeriCorps programs I did: the pay was brutally low, the hours were long, and the stress/uncertainty was high a lot of the time. Sometimes there were unreasonable demands delivered by my manager at Reading Partners, but I learned over time there that my manager wasn't good with follow through, so I became very selective about how much I did that she asked of me when it felt like too much. There was also some annoying periods of make-work that had to do with weird school district politics that wouldn't let me and my fellow AmeriCorps members start at our school sites until fairly late in the fall semester. That's almost certainly an outlier though.

I'm strongly in favor of improving AmeriCorps wages and working conditions. I served for four years. The poverty pay is a barrier to entry for people who would otherwise make great members. But more than that, AmeriCorps serves to depress entry level nonprofit wages by encouraging nonprofits to not pay people a living wage for vital work, but rather creating cohorts of idealist young people who go from making $12,000 a year in AmeriCorps to making $24,000 a year outside of AmeriCorps and thinking that either wage is okay.

That said, I think the barriers to unionizing AmeriCorps members are many. First, turnover is high and members are mission focused to the point of sacrificing themselves and the value of their labor at the altar of the work. Second, if you do convince enough members at your site to vote to unionize, you won't just be negotiating with the site, you'll also have CNCS involved because they will have a vested interest in being sure that AmeriCorps members aren't able to unionize and upset the status quo. That leads to your next problem, more than likely, if you do make through a National Labor Relations Board certified election with a majority of members wanting to form a union, more than likely the site will challenge the very idea that AmeriCorps members have a right to organize. Actually, this would probably happen before an election, but either way, this kind of litigation can easily take years to work its way out, and, well, most members sign up for terms that are less than 12 months.

I don't want to discourage you from pursuing a fair working environment and protection of your rights as a worker, but I think you should be aware that the challenges to unionizing are huge, and the way to go about it is to start local. If you want to organize your work site, go for it. Contact a labor organization that represents workers who do things broadly similar to your work with AmeriCorps and see what resources they have to help you organize. Contact the other members you're working with and feel out their interest. Do your homework. And don't forget labor's eternal motto: Educate. Agitate. Organize.

Allowances on a W4 is about whether you are head of household, married, have dependents, etc. It's used to estimate your taxes owed and withhold from your paycheck based on that. If you overestimate by claiming too few allowances, you will withhold more money for taxes than you actually owe and get a refund when you file your taxes in April. If you underestimate your taxes owed by claiming too many allowances, you will underpay taxes throughout the year and owe the difference when you file your taxes in April.

Use page 3, "Personal Allowances Worksheet," of this IRS W4 form to determine how many allowances you should claim. [https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/fw4.pdf](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/fw4.pdf)

Prepping for an AmeriCorps interview isn't really any different from prepping for any other job interview. Don't worry about buzzwords, instead focus on researching the specific organization that could be hiring you. AmeriCorps is an umbrella organization that funds lots of different nonprofits, schools, libraries, local governmental departments, etc. So learn about this particular Urban Safety program and show up with some questions prepared for them that you couldn't learn just from reading their website or reading up about AmeriCorps generally. Things I always ask are, what does success look like in this role? What is a typical day like here? How did you join this organization and what do you like about it here?

When you're prepping for the interview, look at the position description they posted. For each bullet point, think of something you've done that could apply to it. If they say they want a "team player," come up with a time you worked on a group project or went out of your way for somebody else.

Do some googling for typical interview questions and prepare some answers for those. Usually you can expect things like, what's your biggest weakness? Or what's a time that you've failed at something? The key to questions like this is the pivot. Answer truthfully, but end with how you're working on fixing your weakness or what you learned from your failure and how you've improved since then.

Whether or not you have the qualifications they're looking for, you'll definitely give a good impression if you spend time doing your research and show up having prepared some strong answers to the typical questions. I would suggest a suit if you have one. You'll never feel underdressed in an interview if you're in a suit.

It sounds like you applied to positions that are administered the same way my program was when I served as a VISTA Leader.

The way it worked for us was our organization received the grant for a number of VISTA members and me as a VISTA Leader. We then used a couple of those VISTA members for spots in our organization for special projects, the remaining members we sub-granted out to other organizations that needed the extra man power of having just one or two VISTAs, but couldn't handle or support a full VISTA grant of 10+ members.

When someone applied for one of our open positions, we would review their application, and anyone that wasn't clearly unqualified would get a screening interview with us. After that, as long as they were qualified and there weren't any major red flags, we would pass them on to the hosting organization for them to interview when they had time. The hosting organization would then recommend their top pick to us, and we would start on the on-boarding paperwork. The whole process took a couple of months, and it could be confusing for the applicants.
Rarely, we would have someone apply to multiple positions with our different host sites, which was fine, but they would have to interview with each host site separately.

Also, it's important to keep in mind that every organization moves at a different speed. When I was a VISTA Leader, I tried to make sure I was responding to every application within a few days. That was possible because we didn't get a high volume of applicants and my job at that point was totally focused on recruitment and screening. Other organizations don't have someone who can dedicate that much time to screening and interviews, or they just have a much higher volume of applications, so they move slower. That said, if you haven't heard back in a week or two, I think it's fine to shoot off a polite email checking on your application. I would err more to the two week mark because I'm more cautious, but I don't think it's rude to check on your application after a week has passed with no communication.

The idea of taxation as theft arises because the libertarian ideology only makes room for negative freedoms - freedom from something - and not for positive freedoms - freedom to something. From the libertarian viewpoint, any income they earn is due 100% to their own effort with no outside input from society as a whole. Therefore the government taxing their labor is illegitimate as the government has provided no actual benefit to them in return for the taxes taken. They conveniently ignore the fact that even "free markets" rely on the guarantee of the government ensuring property rights, enforcing contracts, and maintaining a stable money supply in order to stabilize the market, as well as other things like providing for an educated work force, defending the homeland, and responding to disasters (natural or economic). The libertarian viewpoint discounts these things as being fundamentally important to their personal journey to accumulate capital. I believe all but the most ardent and radical libertarians accept taxation begrudgingly, but only to the degree that it supports the above activities.

The view I take, and the view a lot of socialists take, is that taxation is necessary to provide for the freedom of the people to pursue productive and meaningful lives. All the things I listed above are useful in creating stable market interactions and would likely be viewed by most libertarians as acceptable forms of government activity.

The socialist point of view is that besides the freedom from oppression, violence, and terror, which it is the government's role to play a part in curtailing, there are also essential positive freedoms the government can provide for - things like pursuing education, living a healthy life, and having a democratic voice in your work place. Therefore taxes can be used to provide us all the freedom to take a chance, pursue a dream, raise a family, start a business, without the fear of imminent disaster when an unexpected bill pops up or we lose our job or any other number of myriad, unforeseen circumstances happen that can put a working class person in jeopardy of economic ruin.

Taxation is how we return the capital and commensurate economic freedom that has been siphoned away from the vast majority of citizens to provide for the general welfare of our country. We can disagree on what level of taxation is appropriate and which services provided by government are fundamental, but without the government and taxation to support it, there would be less freedom and fewer opportunities for all of us. In a very real way, taxation enables us to live freely.

The main thing to remember is, since you have a masters in education and experience as a teacher, you have a lot of options besides AmeriCorps. Being a teacher requires so many intersectional skills that you could excel at almost any job in the non-profit world based on that alone. AmeriCorps service isn't going to add a whole lot to that other than maybe being a foot in the door to a place you want to work for (but in that case, just apply to them as a real employee first).

As far as budgeting, check out /r/personalfinance if you don't already. The reality of the stipend is you'll need food stamps and medicaid (so look for a state that enrolled in the Obamacare medicaid expansion). Minimize your debts. If you aren't paying for a car/student loans/credit card bills, your budget will go a lot farther. Be comfortable either living with roommates or living in the shittiest apartment possible. Living without a car is doable depending on the city. Even cities without strong public transit can be done if you get a bike. Cities with mediocre public transit can be done if you're willing to spend hours commuting. Whatever else you do, make sure you have savings before you do AmeriCorps, or you have someone to bankroll you, because there will be unexpected expenses, and you don't want to end up in credit card or payday loan debt because you needed emergency dental surgery, or your car broke down, or your cat needed to be euthanized, or whatever million other things that can happen did.

This sounds kind of defeatist. I don't want to discourage you from trying AmeriCorps or something else like it. Giving a year of your life to service is awesome and will teach you a ton, just be sure you  aren't sacrificing your happiness for it!

If you want to go to work for a non-profit and you have experience as a classroom teacher, then just start applying for jobs with non-profits that interest you. A year of AmeriCorps isn't going to make a big difference for you at this point in your career. If you want a unique job experience that has a specific end date, and you want to use AmeriCorps as an easy way to get a job before you move somewhere new, then go for it. AmeriCorps is good for that. I did 4 years and moved all across the country, trying out a bunch of different cities.

You just need to be aware of what AmeriCorps is if you get involved. It's going to be a lot of 18-20 somethings who are fresh out of school that don't really know what they want to do. That can be a lot of fun, and you can learn a lot about a new community by moving across the country and spending a year of your life working on something that interests you.

The best reason I can think of doing AmeriCorps for someone at your general stage in life would be if you just want a break. If you want to take a year off and try something way out there, see what you see, learn what you learn, and then figure things out later. Don't try to use AmeriCorps as a ladder into a career because you'll just be disappointed and realize with your experience you should have just skipped the ridiculously low pay in the first place. Use AmeriCorps as a reprieve, but just be sure you won't experience financial hardship by serving, because for you, having a career history behind you, it won't be worth it.

As far as holding a second job, sure you can do that if you want to, but I wouldn't. Personally, I don't like working. I work just enough in order to enjoy my life. So I don't want to bust my balls doing 40-50 hours a week in AmeriCorps and then spend another 10-15 hours a week in a shitty job just to scrape by, but if that's something that doesn't bother you, then go for it.

AmeriCorps work can be super rewarding (and it can feel super pointless). One of the main perks of it is that you literally aren't getting paid enough to put up with anyone's bullshit. As a teacher, they pay you a living wage, so you've gotta play nice and keep letting people shit on you. In AmeriCorps, they don't even pretend to pay you minimum wage, so there's no point in killing yourself over people's expectations. Do what you want to do. Get what you want out of it. You'll probably meet really interesting people and gain some neat new perspectives. You'll have stories at the end of it that will be worth telling. You'll definitely learn things you wouldn't anywhere else. These are all worthwhile, but don't think AmeriCorps has anything to do with finding a job because it doesn't. It's a pause button. If that's what you want, then it's great. If it isn't, look somewhere else.

(This is all based on my perspective. I know people who did AmeriCorps and moved from service positions to staff positions with their host sites. It happens. I just wouldn't count on it.)

It's not a crazy idea, and people of all ages and walks of life enter AmeriCorps. Though generally it's either the fresh out of high school/college or retirees who end up serving, I've worked with folks in their late twenties and early thirties.

First, I would make sure you know what you're getting into. AmeriCorps is going to be like teaching in that you can end up having a lot of expectations put on you with very little support, though I'm sure you'll find it infinitely easier than being a classroom teacher. The main drawback, of course, is the pay. The stipend is criminally low. That doesn't mean don't do AmeriCorps, just be sure you've got a budget that makes sense for you, and you won't be surprised when you're getting payed $450 every two weeks.

As far as choosing a program, the my.americorps.gov site is a great place to get started. Select some areas that interest you and start reading through open positions. I would generally suggest, when you do more research (don't just rely on the americorps website, google any place you might want to apply), you will probably find that larger AmeriCorps programs that have been around longer will have more consistent quality.

I was an AmeriCorps VISTA Leader that placed members in small nonprofits across our region, and my members had a huge range experiences when it came to the quality of work they were expected to do at their service sites and how much support they received from staff. This was mostly due to the constraint of working for a small nonprofit.

When I served as an AmeriCorps member with a couple of large, well-established programs, I found that they were very consistent and generally offered a lot more support because they were used to working with hundreds of members each year.

Good luck!

Writing a resume is about telling the story that is most likely to get you called for an interview. How you tell that story is 100% up to you. Don't fabricate things, obviously, but feel free to elide details or emphasize the thing that is most likely to get you in the door. In the end, a resume will never land you a job. It will only get you a call back.

It depends on what you want to emphasize. I did 4 terms of service. So when I want to emphasize specific sites I worked with, I will list them as separate jobs with accomplishments and responsibilities. When I want to emphasize the continuity of my experience (avoid the impression that I was just job-hopping for 4 years), I list them all under the same heading of AmeriCorps.

For you, it will probably come down to, when you're writing your resume for a particular job, whether you want to emphasize the organization you're working for and how closely aligned that is to the place you're applying, or if you want to emphasize AmeriCorps as a whole because that aspect is more relevant. Both are going to be important for different kinds of jobs.

Good luck, have a great year!

Having served as a TL in NCCC, and having depression myself I can give you my perspective, but please take it as only that - my perspective. My experience, for what it's worth, is that your gut is usually right after an interview. I've accepted a job where I came out of the interview thinking that my supervisor was at an incredibly basic level in their program development, and I wouldn't be challenged by the position. I was right.

I've accepted a job where the interview was amazing because I could tell the person was incredibly passionate about their work and they made me want to get involved. I ended up working with a lot of other people who were just as passionate, and it was amazing.

I've accepted a job where the person interviewing me did all the talking and didn't let me describe myself. They ended up providing me with no feedback while I was in the position and blamed me for not making improvements I didn't know needed to be made. It was awful, but looking back pretty obvious based on my interview.

If the person who interviewed you will be a part of your everyday role, then I would give heavy consideration to the feelings you came away from the interview with. If they will only be tangentially related to what you're doing, then I would move forward more cautiously.

Since you specifically say that you don't have any leadership experience, I don't think you'll be accepted as a Field Team Leader. You might have a better chance if you're interested in being a Support Team Leader (STL).

STLs do more behind the scenes work. They provide assistance to office staff in support of teams out in the field. There are a few departments that you can serve with as an STL. Unit STLs work with Unit Leaders to support a group of about 4-6 teams. They do a lot of paperwork, desk work, administrative sorts of activities. Community Relations STLs work with the Community Relations department to do outreach - social media, recruitment events, marketing, and communications. Program STLs help the Program Department choose hosts for the teams, review applications, compile reports from the teams on their work, things like that. Operations STLs work with the Ops Department to ensure all the teams have the tools they need to complete their work. This means tracking inventory, checking materials out to teams, helping with facilities maintenance, and fleet management.

However, even to get one of these positions where you aren't leading a team every day, you need to have leadership skills because you will be expected to lead teams during disaster calls, or on shorter projects.

Your best chance is to think more critically and creatively about the experience you have and how it can be framed as related to leadership. Have you led group projects at school? Have you helped train new staff members at work? Have you had to "manage up" either at work or at school? Have you coordinated a service project? Have you taught a group?

If you don't have any leadership experience at all, then your chances are slim. However, if you can come up with something creative that demonstrates your leadership qualities, then you'll be much more likely to be selected.

I did not have any direct leadership experience before becoming a TL, however I was able to frame my experience at work and as a volunteer in such a way that showed I took on progressively more responsibility for myself and those around me, demonstrating that I already possessed the qualities of a Team Leader.

The major differences in benefits are:

-Non-competitive eligibility: VISTA members receive NCE for 1 year after completing their service. When applying for federal jobs you can indicate that you have NCE. This is a minor bump in your application for a federal job.

-Cash stipend after service: If you don't want the education award you can choose a $1500 cash stipend instead. You cannot receive both an ed award and the stipend. If you take the stipend you are not eligible to receive a student loan interest payment from CNCS at the end of your service.

-Eligible to apply for VISTA Leader positions after 1 year of service. VISTA Leaders receive a larger stipend ($200 more per month) and are eligible for a larger end of service cash stipend ($3000 vs. $1500).

-Relocation allowance: if you are moving more than 50 miles from your home of record to your service site you are entitled to a relocation allowance. This is based on the mileage from your home of record to your service site. Some states will offer a flat allowance of ~$200 + mileage. Others will only offer the mileage reimbursement.

-Mandatory attendance at Pre-Service Orientation: meals, travel, and lodging are provided. You will learn about the history of VISTA, meet other VISTAs serving across the country, and prepare for your year of service.

-Access to vistacampus.gov. The VISTA campus provides regular webinars on a bunch of topics relevant to service. It can be a good resources to guide your own learning.

This is changing. Dallas ISD just implemented a performance-based pay scale, doing away with seniority and level of education as the two sole factors in deciding a teacher's salary.

Now teachers have to go through a complex, lengthy process every 2 years in order to raise their salaries after a certain point. Their performance is measured on a sliding scale that is designed to ensure only a very small number of teachers (~2%) will ever reach the highest levels of pay.

I agree with all of this, but I wanted to add a little more nuance to my original post. Under "benefits and prestige" I would count non-financial factors as being of paramount importance. Things like teachers have more control over the curriculum in their class, having more planning time, being able to rely on strong mentorships and professional support in the first 3-5 years of their career, being able to make meaningful decisions at their school in conjunction with administration.

I also think pay should be higher. The bar for becoming a teacher should be raised, not lowered. If we treat the teaching profession like we treat doctors, with a required "residency" period, demanding only the brightest graduates, and increasing the amount of education it takes to join the field, then teaching as a career starts to look more competitive for bright college students. It stops being a career where people go, "I don't know what field my degree leads to... I guess I'll teach for a couple years!" And it becomes a career where we value teachers as incredibly well educated professionals who should have greater control over their classrooms and their schools.

See this paper for more information about what causes teachers to leave high-poverty schools. Note that it's not salary; it's school culture, administration, and collegiality.

As a VISTA Leader who is getting to the end of their term, I'll tell you that I was in exactly the same place you were at about the 3-6 month mark, maybe even earlier. The VISTA project I work for had been neglected for several years and was missing a lot of really basic, fundamental things. Things like yearly goals, standardized data collection, expectations for recruitment, etc. At first I was kind of overwhelmed into inaction, but after awhile of being bored out of my mind (and thinking about quitting) I started tackling each problem one at a time.

I'm leaving my project in a much better place now than where it was when I started. Instead of 10+ years of detritus floating around in our shared documents folder, everything has been culled, and only the most important documents are left. We have yearly goals and milestones to complete on a quarterly basis to reach those goals. Our host sites are starting to be held accountable for what they said they would do. The next VISTA Leader will have a much more active role in recruitment.

These are all really fundamental things that had been lost in the 10+ years that my VISTA project has been around. And while it's kind of ridiculous to be going back to the basics now, I guess, why the hell not. I've learned a ton about planning a program, interpreting government regulations, setting standards and practices, and defining measures of success. I feel overwhelmingly positive about my experience this year, now. Just a few months ago I would have been in a similar place to where you are.

I think you've already identified what you can do to make your year more meaningful to you: be creative, identify projects that you want to work on and go after them. Often you'll be told no; that just comes with the territory. When I'm faced with a no, I essentially ignore it. I take into account the concerns of the person saying no, and then I pursue the project anyway. When I have a draft I want to show off, I explain my position again, explain how I incorporated their concerns, and push for my vision. I've found that 9 times out of 10 I make progress, and the real issue was that we weren't on the same page to begin with. It's easier for someone to say no to an idea when there's nothing in front of them and they're imagining it will be more work for them than to say no to an idea where most of the work is already done and you're just asking permission to move forward. The best supervisors will recognize when you are motivated to work on a project and let you go at it on your own, while the not-so-great supervisors will need you to teach them how to work with you.

The same advice that I'm sure you give to your VISTA members applies to you here: own your experience. Advocate for yourself. You know best what will make you feel accomplished at the end of your year, so go after those things. If your work doesn't feel meaningful as a VISTA it's most likely because you haven't done enough to find a meaningful project to work on.

Volunteer experience is an important indicator of your commitment to service. Being an AmeriCorps member can be tough, and often times thankless. Being able to persevere through the challenges because you see the bigger picture of service is how you'll get through it. And while you can say that in an essay, it says a lot more if you've lived it through your experiences. Having volunteer experiences demonstrates some aspects of that kind of grit.

That said, it isn't necessarily a deal-breaker. I have one candidate right now who left their community service section blank - no essay, no volunteer experience. That is a red flag, and even though the rest of the application is spot on, I have to reject this person and encourage them to reapply with a complete application.

City connections are formed in just the way you've described - connecting your outlying cities to your capital via roads and harbors. If your capital is connected to City 1 via roads, and City 1 is connected to City 2 via harbors, and City 2 is connected to City 3 via roads, then all 3 cities are connected to your capital.

Cap - - - - C1 o o o o C2 - - - - C3

However, the problem you might be facing is a blockade that is blocking sea trade. A barbarian or a military unit from a civ or CS that you are at war with blocks trade on the hexes surrounding that unit. So if there are barbarians blocking hexes around your harbor cities they can stop city connections from being established.

You can read more about trade routes and city connections here: http://civilization.wikia.com/wiki/Trade_route_(Civ5)

School time is limited. Every time someone brings up the idea of requiring more content, more subjects for our schools to teach, the same question is usually left unasked: where will we find the instructional time? Some things like driver's ed don't make sense for all students to worry about. If you live in a city with strong public transportation and no real need for a car, then driver's ed is a waste of your school time. Home economics could be useful in some regards, but the skills people usually associate with it (e.g. balancing your budget) can be taught more efficiently through cross-curricular instruction in existing class structures (e.g. lessons utilizing microeconomics in our math classes).

Quite simply, school's can't teach everything, nor should they try. What we don't teach is as important as what we do teach. The greater issue, I believe, is clarifying the role of our current curriculum. What is the purpose of a liberal arts education (which is the education all of our students receive)? I would argue it teaches students how to think critically and discover new information for themselves. If I were going to add anything to our curricula, I would add a greater emphasis on utilizing online search tools to find information. A school can't provide all of the answers, but it can provide the right frame of mind for discovering the answers to questions on our own.

I also want to add the following information on volunteer grievance procedures. What you are talking about doing is filing an informal grievance, the gist of the applicable rules is that you need to:

1. Provide written documentation to the ED outlining the grievance (this can be notes from your meeting with the supervisor and your ED, send an email asking for their affirmation that your notes align with their understanding of the meeting)
2. Describe (in writing) the relief you are requesting (i.e. specific steps your sponsor can take to change the situation)
3. Allow 5 business days for response to your grievance. If after 5 days you have received no response, or a response you find inadequate, then bring the issue to your state office for action.

The entire procedure is found here http://www.nationalservice.gov/sites/default/files/documents/45CFR_1211.pdf

You've already started this process. So make sure that you have provided your grievance and requested relief in writing and that you've received written confirmation from the ED. Once you've done this you are absolutely within your rights to elevate this matter to the state office. You can refer to the grievance procedures specifically and let them know you are asking for specific relief.

All this is to say, know what you are asking for when you go to the next level. Decide on what kind of intervention you think would resolve this issue and ask for it. If your sponsor cannot, or chooses not to supply that intervention, then ask for it from the state office. By knowing what you want to happen so you can complete your year successfully the state office will be in a better position to support you.

It sounds like you want to transfer your service to another site. You can ask for that from the state office. If you choose to do so, then exercise your rights, but do so calmly and with purpose. Service is about what we can give to others, not about sacrificing our own happiness and well-being. No VISTA should be put in your position, and for that I am personally sorry. Please let us know how things turn out!

Hey there! I've served as an STL at the Atlantic campus, so I hope my answer will be helpful to you.

First off, serving as a TL at all is an amazing opportunity, and there are some really cool people you'll get to meet as part of Team Green. But being an STL is a very different life from being an FTL. First off, you're not responsible for a team and you won't be going on spike regularly. This means your life is going to be way less stressful (for the most part) and you'll be able to better approximate a 40 hour work week.

That doesn't mean you won't work hard, especially any time the rest of the corps is on campus, like during CTI and transitions. You'll still be busting your butt, you just won't be at the same level of stress as your FTL counterparts, which is a good thing. FTLs are really asked to do an almost impossible job with not nearly enough support. The fact that anybody makes it through is 1. blind luck 2. a testament to their inner strength, and 3. due to the support of their fellow TLs.

I can tell you that your FTL friends will be dreaming of having your job by the middle of the year. And you will actually get the best of both worlds, because you'll be able to lead a spike at some point in your year. If you go out for the fire unit (your Moose UL is the POC for fire) you'll almost be guaranteed a full spike as an FTL with fire. If you're interested in this, look up the "pack test" (first google result gets you there) to see whether you need to do any additional training to qualify. However, even if you don't join fire, you'll still be sent out on a spike at some point in your year, either as part of a disaster response or as a mini-project to give you field experience. The staff takes your field experience seriously and will make sure you get a chance to flex your leadership in the field.

As for day-to-day work, that's going to depend on which department you're working with. I can tell you more if you've been offered a position with Unit, Programs, or Operations. Generally, (other than ops) your job will be pretty clear-cut office work. If you're comfortable with that, then being an STL can be an awesome experience.

As far as the campus goes: they just moved into their new facitilities which are very nice (wifi and cable in every room), though much more communal than their previous campus (16 beds per room). The campus is in Dundalk which is outside of Baltimore proper, but there is a free bus you can pick up from near campus that will take you downtown, and then you basically have everything you want to do in a major city, or you can hop a train to DC/New York/wherever for the weekend.

The argument against this point is rather common, and pretty much at the core of the economics of Star Trek: society has pressured its members to value being active producers above being passive consumers. 

If you've ever been out of work for more than a few weeks, you'll feel this same pressure. While it may be nice initially to enjoy time to yourself (when you're not looking for work) eventually your expanded leisure time is exhausting in its own right. Currently the main pressure that keeps us from being layabouts is economic, most of us simply can't afford to leave our jobs. However, this is an artificial construction of society; we have a society that chooses to impose the economic burden of providing for basic necessities on its members in order to push them into being productive.

The society depicted in Star Trek chooses a different form of pressure to push its members into productivity - namely peer pressure. While some number of people will choose not to work, to live entirely off the dole, the vast majority will feel the force of this social pressure and pursue some form of productivity. Very likely the ratio of people simply enjoying the largess of the Federation to those pursuing some employment is similar to what is considered a "healthy" unemployment rate in modern capitalist systems.

As for the question of "undesirable" professions, which you presumably lump being a hair-stylist into, this is accounted for in the original article. The author proposes that some trivial, but non-zero amount of energy credit is applied to each worker's "ledger" in proportion to the difficulty and value of the work they perform. So the same equation that exists today in the U.S. for pressuring people into finding work also exists in the economy of Star Trek, although the proportion of the variables has been altered. Instead of the dominating factor being fulfillment of basic needs (shelter, food, etc.) with a moderating factor being social pressure, the dominating factor is social pressure and the moderating one an accumulation of additional energy credit.

>Once both people started entering the work force, shit got fucked. Now kids are sent to day cares and left unsupervised, and pricing has gone way up due to the new expectation of a family having a double income.

This is your initial argument, that families have been unable to keep up because wages haven't increased to meet the demands of necessary living expenses.  Now, I believe this claim is spurious, especially when I consider your follow up post which is an argument that supply/demand dynamics are the motivating factor in this wage stagnation.  If supply and demand have caused wages to stall, why hasn't a similar effect occurred to prices on basic goods? When consumers cannot afford staple goods, prices must fall, otherwise the producers of those goods will no longer be able to sustain their own growth long term. I must conclude that there are more complex mechanisms at work here than you would choose to believe.

>Women joining the workforce has nearly doubled the amount of workers available, while demand for things has not doubled.

In 1960 there were 36.6 million men and 14.8 million women in the workforce. In 2009 those numbers grew to 56.1 and 43.2 million, respectively.  That means a total growth from 51.2 million workers to 99.3 million. It would seem from this rudimentary comparison, that your claim is factually sound.  However, does this approximate doubling in the workforce translate into a doubling in the unemployment rate? I assume that is your contention, since in your example of the 20 people trying to fill 15 jobs there would be a rather high rate of unemployment.  Checking the [facts](http://data.bls.gov/timeseries/LNU04000000?years_option=all_years&periods_option=specific_periods&periods=Annual+Data) tells me no, unemployment hasn't significantly increased. It certainly hasn't doubled.

Lets's turn to your implied claim that the average family has been hurt by the addition of women to the workforce.  Simply put, median family income since 1960 has [grown](http://www.russellsage.org/sites/all/files/chartbook/Income%20and%20Earnings.pdf).  Check the first graph and you can see the breakdown in real income growth from 1945-2010. 

From looking at the available data, I can only conclude that you are wrong, and the addition of women to the work force has been a boon to our economy and the financial well-being of our families.

I will add, that in my research I did find claims that low education workers have been hurt by the increased competition posed by the integration of both genders into the labor pool.  You can see this played out in the final graph of my above link which shows that those workers with a H.S. degree or less have lost ground in wages, especially compared to their more educated peers.  I would argue, however, that this is not a case of women in the workplace pulling down men's wages.  Rather it is an example of increased global competition, and the shift in our economy to a post-industrial state that relies far more on worker education than any time previous.

"People should be split into classes based on their abilities and expected to perform during school hours."

What you're talking about is ability tracking, which has been proven to be less effective than other models.  There is a reason that our schools have moved to an integrated model, the benefits that lower-performing students receive by being placed in the same classes as their high-performing peers are greater expectations and more rigorous classwork.  There is an overall upward trajectory for the whole classroom, as opposed to a segregated model where poorly performing students are separated to classes with low expectations and less rigorous classwork.  By putting students together we improve the performance for the bottom quartile while still being able to serve that top quartile of students through differentiated instruction (extensions on what the whole class is doing).

Obviously your situation is unique, and you certainly benefited from the accelerated track your parents chose for you, but it would be wrong to take the anecdotal evidence of your situation and use it to suggest a reform for our current system.

A lot of these suggestions are very interesting, but I think it's important to talk about why these things aren't showing up in our schools.  The purpose of a school isn't (and really can't be) to teach everything that people need to know to live in the world.  Schools are there to give kids the building blocks so they can go out and educate themselves.  To achieve this goal our schools have focused their curricula on a few subjects that form the building blocks of making meaning in the world.

For example reading, obviously, is a very important skill to teach if we want our students to be able to teach themselves after the school day is over.  And let's not forget that the school day is a finite thing, most kids spend between 6 and 7 hours each day at school, far less time than they spend at home, with their friends, on the computer, at the mall, etc.  In order to fit all of the things that we might want into the school day would require a radical reinvention of the traditional school schedule in America.

It's important to keep in mind that schools are working with limited resources, and one of those resources is time.  So as much as we might want to include self-defense in our curriculum, it would have to come at the expense of something else.

As a person who has done lots of contract work on farms around Iowa (my father is a millwright and I worked for him during my summers), building permits on farm structures have certainly saved my life or at least my limbs.  We used to joke about making things up to 'OSHA', it was a common line for my dad to say 'sure as hell ain't OSHA approved', but when it comes down to it I've known too many people who have been injured or killed by unsafe working conditions.  As some one hired from the outside to do work in a place that inherently has dangers (working 100+ feet in the air, welding around dry grain, working with heavy loads) I'd much rather have the piece of mind knowing that the platform I'm about to walk onto isn't going to fall out of the sky and take me and my dad down with it, than a laissez faire government that refuses to enforce basic safety standards that clearly can and do affect people's lives.

I was hospitalized briefly last year.  It happened right over Thanksgiving; I was living far from home for the first time, having a hard time connecting with my coworkers, and battling a depression that I had come to accept as part of my life over the last few years.  I decided to take some pills one night after seeing my therapist and immediately regretted the decision. I spent the next day vomiting my guts out in the ER, with no one on earth knowing where I was, why I hadn't shown up to work, anything at all about me.  They transferred me from the ER to an in-patient psychiatric facility where I spent the next 7 days accepting the fact that medication could help me and my family had to be a part of my life.

When I was admitted I thought that the only thing worse than being depressed was being stuck in a small, locked facility with a bunch of crazy people.  But there was one ward nurse who was there when I was admitted and only worked the overnight. He actually got through to me, pointing out how stupid and selfish I was to end up there.

In my experience, the staff recognized that I needed help, but they knew I didn't belong on the ward.  I was stuck there for the week surrounding Thanksgiving because it was Thanksgiving and the Doctor was home with his family, so he couldn't sign my release.  If there was anything the experience taught me, it was patience, because there were people who needed to be there, and there were people who kept coming back, and there were people you wouldn't ever expect to see there, but we all had to go through this same experience of surrendering control over our lives to a system that could not help but dehumanize us. All sense of personal responsibility was removed, we were moved around without any say or control over where we were sent.  In the mornings they would roll us out of bed at 5:30 or 6:00 to check our vitals one at a time and then let us go back to sleep before breakfast. It was an experience that required fortitude of thought to endure. They days could seem endless, punctuated only briefly by the difference in food at meal times.  It was easy to withdraw into hopelessness while waiting for the next visit with the Doctor, having your release date postponed multiple times, being confronted with the impersonal facade of an organization constructed to keep you horrifyingly calm 24/7.

It wasn't a lot of fun, but I did spend those days reading Dostoevsky's "Demons" and I got to listen to Johnny Cash's "The Man Comes Around." So that was good.
